prompts.L3:
Please expand the following bullet points into a complete, well-structured text:

- The speaker acknowledges John’s anger and pain over his wife leaving in the night before being sold south.
- The speaker challenges John for not seeming worried because he is free while his wife faces being sold away.
- The speaker says she has secured a small but clean room in Philadelphia where they can live together.
- The speaker imagines making a home with John and children where they can both be truly free.
- The speaker gives John a new suit, calling it clothing fit for a free man.
prompts.L4:
Please expand the following two-sentence summary into a complete text:

A woman addresses John about the pain and danger of family separation under slavery, urging escape by offering a room in Philadelphia, a new suit, and the promise of building a free home together. Her appeal shows that freedom means more than legal status: it means safety, dignity, love, and liberation from the constant threat of sale and violence.
prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: john lord knows

outputs.L1:
John, Lord knows you are still vexed. I reckon I would be too if my wife stole away during the sleepy night, when God and the devil seem the only souls awake. Even if I knew she was about to be sold south, even if I knew she was leaving—and you did know.

You grow so troubled when I speak of leaving. Call me a fool, call me Cudjo, but I have been five years with you, John. Your wife is about to be sold away, and just because you are free, does that not worry you at all? You laugh, and I do not know if I would miss your laugh if I were in the South.

Thank you, Jesus, I have a room in Philadelphia, John. It is not large, but it is clean—enough room for us, and for some children too. Your baby, John. I am not too old yet, just around thirty-one, I think. Let us make a home, John, one where we are both free: free from the shadow of the lash, free as the Lord intended.

I have this suit for you, John. No one has worn these clothes before. Walk proudly in them. These are a free man’s clothes.
outputs.L2:
John, the Lord knows you are still angry. I suppose I would be too if my wife slipped away in the middle of the night, when only God, the devil, and restless souls are awake.

Even if I knew she was about to be sold down South. Even if I understood she was leaving, just as you did.

You get so upset whenever I speak of going. You call me foolish. You call me Cudjo. Five years with you, John, and your wife is about to be taken and sold away. Just because you are free, does that mean it does not trouble you? You laugh—but I do not know if I would miss that laugh if I were in the South.

Still, thank Jesus, I have found a room in Philadelphia. It is not large, but it is clean enough, with space for us and maybe some children too. Your baby—I am not too old yet, only about thirty-one, I think.

We could build a home there, John. A place where we would both be free. Free from the shadow of the lash. Free the way the Lord intended.

I brought this suit for you, John. No one has ever worn these clothes before. Stand tall in them. These are the clothes of a free man.
outputs.L3:
The speaker begins by acknowledging John’s anger and pain. She understands how deeply he is suffering after learning that his wife left in the night, just before she was to be sold south. She recognizes that such a loss is not only heartbreaking but also terrifying, because being sold away could mean permanent separation.

At the same time, the speaker challenges John’s reaction. She questions why he does not seem more worried about his wife’s fate, especially now that he himself is free while she remains in danger of being carried far away. To the speaker, John’s freedom should not make him forget the suffering of the woman he loves. Instead, it should make him more determined to help her.

The speaker then reveals that she has made practical plans for their future. She has secured a small room in Philadelphia, modest but clean, where they can live together. Though it is not grand, it represents safety, stability, and the possibility of beginning again.

She imagines a life there with John, building a real home together. In that home, they could raise children and live not as property, but as human beings with dignity. She dreams of a future in which both of them can be truly free—not only free in body, but free to love, work, rest, and belong to one another without fear of being separated.

Finally, the speaker gives John a new suit of clothes. She presents it as more than a gift; she calls it clothing fit for a free man. The suit symbolizes a new beginning for John, a visible sign of the life he might now claim for himself. Through this gesture, she urges him to step fully into freedom and into the responsibilities that come with it.
outputs.L4:
A woman speaks directly to John about the suffering that slavery has brought into their lives, especially the terrible danger that families can be separated at any moment. She reminds him that under slavery, a husband, wife, parent, or child can be sold away without warning, leaving behind grief, fear, and uncertainty. Her words carry both love and urgency. She does not speak of freedom as an abstract idea, but as something necessary for survival.

She urges John to escape, offering him practical help and a vision of a better life. In Philadelphia, she tells him, there is a room waiting for him, a new suit to wear, and the possibility of beginning again. These details matter because they represent more than comfort. The room offers shelter and safety. The suit offers dignity and a new identity beyond enslavement. Together, they suggest the chance to build a home where no master can threaten them, no auction block can divide them, and no violence can control their future.

Her appeal is also deeply personal. She is not simply asking John to run away; she is inviting him to imagine a life with her in freedom. She speaks of building a home together, one shaped by love rather than fear. In this future, they would no longer live under the constant threat of being sold, beaten, or separated. They would be able to belong to themselves and to each other.

Through her plea, the meaning of freedom becomes much larger than legal status. Freedom is not only the absence of chains or the right to live in a free state. It is the ability to sleep without terror, to love without fear of separation, and to work for one’s own future. It is the restoration of dignity, the protection of family, and the chance to live as a full human being. Her words reveal that escape is not merely a flight from slavery; it is a movement toward safety, self-respect, love, and a life no longer ruled by violence.
outputs.L5:
**John, the Lord Knows**

John walked quietly through the old village, carrying more questions than answers. People often wondered what troubled him, but John rarely spoke about the thoughts that filled his mind. He had faced difficult days, made mistakes, and lost things he once believed would last forever.

Still, whenever life felt uncertain, John reminded himself of one simple truth: **the Lord knows**.

The Lord knows the struggles hidden behind a calm face. He knows the prayers whispered in the dark, the hopes that remain unspoken, and the pain that others cannot see. For John, this belief became a source of comfort. It helped him keep going when the road ahead seemed unclear.

John learned that he did not need to understand everything at once. He only needed faith, patience, and the courage to take one step at a time. If people misunderstood him, the Lord knew his heart. If the future felt confusing, the Lord knew the way.

And so John continued forward, not because life was easy, but because he trusted that he was never truly alone. The world might not always understand, but **the Lord knows**.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a raw, unpunctuated dramatic monologue in African American Vernacular English from an enslaved woman speaking to a free Black man named John, urging him to leave with her for Philadelphia before she is sold South.
counterfactuals.output:
John you hear me

dont you turn your face from me now

I been quiet so long my own tongue feel strange in my mouth but I got to speak tonight cause come morning they say I go South and everybody know what that mean

South mean gone

South mean the road eat your name

South mean the sun beat you down till even God got to squint to see you

John I aint going quiet

I aint folding my hands and letting them count my teeth and my hips and my hands like I aint born from no woman like I aint got breath like I aint got a soul that know its own shape

you free

you got paper saying so

you walk with your head up when the patrol pass though I see your hand shake after

you know the streets beyond here

you know the wagon road

you know the river

you know them Quaker folks up toward Philadelphia that say a body can hide in plain sight if they make it past the line

so come with me

dont tell me it too far

dont tell me night too black

dont tell me dogs got nose and men got guns

I know all that

I know fear so well it sleep beside me

I know the sound of keys

I know the smell of the yard at daybreak when they bring somebody out and everybody got to look and nobody allowed to cry too loud

I know what this place do to a woman

I know what they mean when they say sold South

John I seen Esther go

I seen her baby reaching with both hands and nobody put him in her arms

I heard her calling till the wagon turned and after that I heard her in my sleep for three years

I aint letting that be me

I aint letting my voice get left in this dirt

I got my mothers scarf tied under my dress

I got corn bread wrapped in cloth

I got two silver buttons Miss Anne never knew I took

I got feet tough enough to bleed and keep moving

what I aint got is time

John look at me

you once said my name like it was something sweet

you once said if the world was made right you would build me a door and not a chain

well the world aint made right

so we got to break us a door

I aint asking you to save me like I cant save myself

I am asking you to walk beside me cause a lone woman on the road got too many eyes laid on her

I am asking cause I trust you with the part of me that still believe morning can be more than a horn blowing and a white man hollering

Philadelphia John

say it with me

Philadelphia

a place where my back belong to me

where my hands can earn bread for my own mouth

where I can sleep and not wake thinking I heard boots

where maybe I stand in a church and sing full voice

where maybe I find a room with a window

where maybe I can laugh and not look over my shoulder to see who want payment for it

come now

before the moon drop

before the rooster tell on us

before them men hitch that wagon and write my life down in somebody else book

if you love me come

if you fear for me come

if you only got pity then keep it

I need legs

I need nerve

I need somebody who know North by the stars and freedom by the smell of cold air

John

I am leaving tonight

with you or without you

but Lord help me I want your hand in mine when the woods close round us

I want to hear you breathing beside me when the dogs start up

I want to reach that city and turn to you and say we made it

not I made it

we made it

so choose now

chain or road

grave or sky

this place or Philadelphia

John

come on
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a historically inspired first-person speech set during slavery, in dialect, where a woman named Cudjo talks to John about freedom, marriage, escaping north, and giving him a new suit as “free man’s clothes.”
counterfactuals.output:
I can write it in a respectful, lightly period-inflected voice rather than exaggerated dialect.

---

John, you listen to me now. I done carried my fear long enough, folded up small in my chest like a ragged cloth. Every morning I wake with the same sun on my face, but it don’t feel like God’s sun when another man say where I can stand, where I can sleep, who I can love, and when I got to bow my head.

I been thinking on freedom, John. Not like a story folks whisper when the candles burn low, but like a road. A real road. Northward. Past the fields, past the patrols, past every hand that think it own us. I know it ain’t easy. I know the dark got teeth. But I rather walk scared toward freedom than stay safe in chains.

And I been thinking on you.

They say we ain’t got no right to marry proper. Say our promises don’t count less some white man write it down, and even then he can tear it up when he please. But my heart know different. Before God, before the night sky, before our own two souls, I take you as mine if you take me as yours. Not as property. Not as something borrowed. As a man. As John.

So I made you this suit.

Don’t laugh now. My stitches ain’t fine like town ladies sew, but every seam got prayer in it. This coat, these trousers, this shirt—I made ’em for the man you going to be when we cross over. Free man’s clothes, John. Clothes for standing straight in. Clothes for walking into a new morning and not lowering your eyes.

When you put ’em on, I want you to remember: freedom ain’t just a place. It’s how you carry yourself when the world been trying all its life to bend you. It’s choosing your own name, your own work, your own wife, your own tomorrow.

Come with me, John. Come north. Come as my husband in the sight of heaven. Come out of this bondage and into whatever hardship freedom brings, ’cause even hard freedom sweeter than a soft cage.

Take the suit. Put it close. When the time come, we don’t look back. We run for the river, for the woods, for the star that points the way. And when morning find us, let it find us moving.

Let it find us free.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a stream-of-consciousness letter with no standard punctuation from an enslaved wife to her husband John, mixing anger, love, fear of being sold South, and hope for a room in Philadelphia.
counterfactuals.output:
John my heart

I speak to you in my head while my hands are in the wash water and while Mistress calls and while the night comes down like a door

I am angry John

I am so angry I feel it in my teeth

They say my name like it belongs in their mouths  
they count my back my arms my womb my breath  
they talk of selling like I am a chair or a mule  
and I hear South whispered in the yard  
South like a pit  
South like no road back  
South like you and me torn clean from this world

I fear it John

I fear waking to a trader at the gate  
I fear the rope and the wagon  
I fear the paper with a price on me  
I fear your face fading because distance is a thief too  
I fear being made to live where no one knows I am your wife

But I love you

I love you in the morning before I open my eyes  
I love you when I bite my tongue so they do not beat me  
I love you when I hide one crust for later and think if John were here I would give him half  
I love you fierce as fire and soft as prayer  
I love you angry too because love ought not have to crawl

Do you remember what you said about Philadelphia

A room John

Just one room

A door we may shut with our own hands  
a bed no one can sell from under us  
a window with free air coming through  
your coat on a peg  
my shawl on a chair  
bread cooling  
water boiling  
our names spoken without fear

I hold that room inside me

When they threaten South I put Philadelphia before my eyes  
when they say girl I say wife inside my chest  
when they say property I say woman  
when they say hush I hear your voice telling me hold on

Do not think I am only sorrow

I am tired yes  
I am afraid yes  
I am full of rage yes  
but I am still here John  
still breathing  
still yours by my own choosing  
still dreaming past their fences

If they take me I will carry you  
if they lock me I will remember the room  
if they sell me South I will not let them own the part of me that knows your hand  
if I get free I will come  
if you get free you come  
and if the Lord has any mercy let us meet in Philadelphia and shut that door behind us

Your wife always

Mary
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: I need a short poetic monologue in the voice of a 31-year-old enslaved Black woman addressing John Lord, saying she has escaped at night, found lodging in Philadelphia, and wants them to build a free life together.
counterfactuals.output:
John Lord, hear me—

I left when the night was deepest,  
when even the trees held their breath.  
I carried no lantern but my wanting,  
no map but the North Star  
and the name of freedom burning in my chest.

Now I have found a small room in Philadelphia,  
four walls that do not claim me,  
a door I may open by my own hand,  
a morning that calls me woman—not property.

Come to me, John.  
Let us lay down fear like an old chain,  
let us build our days from honest bread,  
warm hands, and chosen names.  
I am thirty-one years alive,  
and at last my life is asking to begin.

Come build it with me.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Write dialogue/monologue for a historical fiction scene: an enslaved woman tells John she knows he is upset she left in the night, but she had to flee being sold south; include dialect, religious references, Philadelphia, children, and a new suit symbolizing freedom.
counterfactuals.output:
“John,” she said softly, standing just inside the doorway, rain darkening the shoulders of the new wool suit she wore. It was plain, brown, and too large at the cuffs, but she held herself in it as if it were velvet. “I know you’re sore with me. I know you woke and found my place empty, and no word left but the cold sheet. Don’t think I don’t know what that done to your heart.”

She drew a breath, steadying herself.

“But I could not stay to be sold South. I heard them plain as church bells—heard my name spoken like I was a chair or a mule. ‘Down to Georgia,’ they said. ‘Maybe New Orleans.’ John, you know what that means. You know women go down there and don’t come back. Mothers parted from their babies. Husbands from wives. Names lost. Graves unmarked. I had the children’s faces before me, every one, and I said to the Lord, ‘If You mean to open a road, I will put my foot on it.’”

Her voice trembled, but did not break.

“I walked by night. Hid by day. Prayed under hedges and in haylofts. More than once I thought my breath itself would give me away. I kept saying the Psalm Mama taught me: ‘Yea, though I walk through the valley of the shadow of death, I will fear no evil.’ And I tell you, John, that valley got mighty long. But the Lord did not leave me in it.”

She touched the sleeve of the suit, almost shyly.

“In Philadelphia, a colored woman at the meetinghouse put this on me. Said I ought not come into freedom wearing the rags they marked me with. Said, ‘Sister, stand up straight now. You belong to God and yourself.’ This suit ain’t fine, but it is mine. First thing I ever wore that no master counted, no mistress handed down, no trader priced with his eye. When I buttoned it, I felt like I was fastening my own soul back into my body.”

She looked at him then, eyes bright with tears and fire.

“I did not leave because I loved you less. I left because I could not let them carry me where you’d never find me. I left because our children—those here, those gone, those yet prayed for—deserve to know their mama was not willing to be driven like cattle to the end of the earth. If freedom was anywhere, I had to run toward it.”

A faint, aching smile touched her mouth.

“So be angry if you must. The Good Lord knows you got cause to grieve. But don’t think I went easy. Every step north, I was saying your name. Every bell I heard in Philadelphia, I wished you heard it too. And when I sat in that church, with colored folks singing like heaven had cracked open, I saved a place beside me in my mind.”

She stepped closer.

“I am here now, John. Not owned. Not sold. Not gone South. Here. And if God be willing, I mean to see you and the children standing in such cloth one day—not just a suit, but freedom itself, cut to fit our own lives.”
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
